Water helps transport minerals present in the soil, such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and calcium.

Similarly, water also transports trace elements such as boron, zinc, and others.

These elements play an essential role in photosynthesis and other vital plant functions.

Water enters the plant through the roots. It carries with it the minerals present in the soil.

It travels up to the leaves through very fine tubes called xylem.

This movement is made possible by a key phenomenon: evapotranspiration.

Evapotranspiration is the loss of water:

through the leaves, via small openings called stomata. This is known as transpiration.

and through the soil, in the form of evaporation.

When water escapes through the stomata, it creates a suction effect, like a pump. The plant then draws water

from the roots to compensate for this loss. This is what causes water to circulate throughout the plant.

👉

pages.title: Capillarity
pages.text:
Root pressure

Other phenomena contribute to this pumping action:

root pressure: pushes water upward.

capillarity: allows water to rise in the xylem.

This system is essential for the plant to transport the water and nutrients it needs.

pages.title: Ultimately, the leaves of plants are a bit like our skin:
pages.text:
They breathe through tiny invisible holes, like the pores in our skin.

They release water, like sweat. If the air is too dry or hot, they lose too much water, just like us when we sweat

a lot.

If we are too hot or haven't drunk enough, we become tired: it's the same for plants!

pages.title: Why add charcoal to the soil?
pages.text: Why add charcoal to the soil?
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Pourquoi ajouter du charbon dans le sol ?

pages.title: Retains water like a sponge
pages.text:
Strengthens crops

Promotes soil life

Ground charcoal, known as biochar, is an excellent ally for:

Water retention: Charcoal acts like a sponge, retaining water and nutrients in its cavities. It stores moisture

and then slowly releases it when the soil is dry. It can retain up to five times its weight in water.

Nourishing the soil: Charcoal provides a refuge for beneficial microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi,

which help plants to feed and enhance soil life.

Strengthening crop resistance: Charcoal improves water retention and soil stability, which helps plants to

better withstand drought.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Retient l’eau comme une éponge

pages.title: OR
pages.text:
Use charcoal that has cooled completely, then grind it finely into powder or small pieces measuring 1 to 10 mm.

If you already have compost ready to use:

Add crushed charcoal at a rate of 10 to 20% of the

total volume. For example: for 1 wheelbarrow of

compost (80 L): add 8 to 16 L of charcoal, or about

1 to 2 buckets.

Mix well for even distribution.

If you make your own compost:

Add a little charcoal to each layer, alternating it

with brown materials (leaves, straw, etc.) and green

materials (kitchen waste, grass clippings, etc.).

Moisten if necessary: charcoal is very absorbent.

Leave to mature.

pages.title: Water is essential to plant life: it enters through the roots, circulates to the leaves, and exits through the stomata.
pages.text:
Understanding this process allows you to water more effectively, at the right time and in the right amount.

With a few simple steps—observing the plant, adjusting watering, mulching the soil, enriching the compost—you

can help your crops grow better, even during dry periods.
